name: Turf toe (1st MTP plantar plate injury)
aka: plantar plate complex injury of the great toe
populations: football players (American football, rugby and soccer), especially on firm or artificial surfaces
running backs and quarterbacks in college football (NCAA surveillance data)
dancers, gymnasts, wrestlers and martial artists
summary: A sprain of the 1st MTP plantar plate complex from forced hyperextension of the great toe, usually on a firm surface. Graded I to III; high-grade injuries risk instability, weak push-off and hallux rigidus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I: back when pain-free with normal weightbearing (traditionally 3–5 days). Grade II: 2–4 weeks lost. Grade III: sources range from 4–6 weeks or more to at least 10–16 weeks, and up to 6 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: NCAA football: mean 10.1 days lost per injury. Operative grade III series (15 football players): mean 16.5 weeks of playing time missed

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Painful, limited great-toe dorsiflexion with plantar tenderness after a hyperextension injury; the vertical Lachman test checks for instability

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weightbearing radiographs with comparison films (sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more suggests plantar plate rupture); MRI to grade the tear

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Clanton and Ford grades I–III, as modified by McCormick and Anderson (sprain, partial tear, complete tear)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 0.062 per 1000 athlete-exposures in NCAA football; fewer than 2% of injuries need surgery

overview:
Turf toe is a sprain of the plantar capsuloligamentous complex of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, caused by forced hyperextension of the great toe [r1,r2]. It was first described in American football players on artificial surfaces, but it also occurs in soccer, basketball, dance and wrestling [r3]. In imaging, the term now usually means a tear of the plantar plate complex [r4].

Most injuries are low-grade and settle within days to weeks, and fewer than 2% need surgery [r5,r3]. The risk lies in missed or high-grade injuries. Unrecognised, they can lead to reduced push-off strength, persistent pain, progressive deformity and eventual joint degeneration [r1]. In an early review, 50% of 20 athletes with a previous turf toe injury had persistent symptoms at more than 5 years [r6]. The evidence is mostly case series and expert reviews, and there are no randomised trials of treatment, so decisions are shared with the athlete.

epidemiology.text: In five seasons of NCAA football surveillance, the incidence of turf toe was 0.062 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 0.052–0.072). Athletes were nearly 14 times more likely to be injured in games than in practice, the mean days lost were 10.1, and fewer than 2% of injuries needed surgery. The rate was higher on third-generation artificial turf than on natural grass (0.087 versus 0.047 per 1000 athlete-exposures), and running backs and quarterbacks were most often injured; most injuries followed contact with the playing surface (35.4%) or another player (32.7%) [r5]. A survey of 80 professional American football players found that 45% had turf toe during their careers, 83% of them on artificial turf [r1]. In rugby, turf toe accounted for 11% of foot injuries in one prospective study, which is about 0.4% of players per season [r1]. The data are mostly from American football and may not apply to other sports.

intrinsic: Reduced great-toe dorsiflexion or a previous first MTP injury (a history of turf toe was associated with lower dorsiflexion in NFL players; whether limited motion is a cause or a result is unknown) [r7]
A bipartite or tripartite sesamoid, which may separate with the same mechanism (case series) [r1]
Playing position: running backs and quarterbacks were the most commonly injured positions in college football [r5]

A plantarflexed ankle with the heel raised at the moment of loading, which puts the load through the forefoot and great toe (Najefi describes the mechanism as an axial load on a hyperextended MTP joint with a fixed equinus position; a chronically tight calf as a risk factor is clinical reasoning and was not tested) [r1]
extrinsic: Firm or artificial playing surfaces: a higher injury rate on third-generation artificial turf than on grass in the NCAA data [r5]; the shoe-surface interface has a significant effect on lower limb injuries, but confounders limit firm conclusions [r8]
Flexible, lightweight footwear that offers poor forefoot support (proposed in early reports; not tested in controlled studies) [r9,r1]
Game exposure and contact: nearly 14 times more likely in games than in practice [r5]
Dance, wrestling and gymnastics, where repeated or forced forefoot hyperextension occurs [r3]

mechanism.summary: The classic mechanism is an axial load on a hyperextended first MTP joint with the ankle plantarflexed and the heel raised, so that the foot is fixed on the surface while the body continues forward, or another player lands on the athlete's heel [r1,r5]. The load forces the great toe into hyperextension beyond its normal range. The plantar plate complex, which resists dorsiflexion, is stretched and then fails, most often distal to the sesamoids at its firm attachment to the base of the proximal phalanx [r1]. Depending on the force direction, the injury can involve the medial or lateral structures and the sesamoids [r1].
sequence: The athlete pushes off, or is planted with the heel raised and the ankle plantarflexed, so the great toe is already extended and the forefoot carries the load [r1].
The forefoot stays fixed on a firm surface while the body keeps moving forward, or another player lands on the heel [r1,r5].
An axial load drives the first MTP joint into forced hyperextension beyond its normal range [r1].
The plantar plate complex, the thickened plantar capsule that resists dorsiflexion, is stretched and attenuates [r1].
It tears, most often distal to the sesamoids; the sesamoid-phalangeal ligaments were the most commonly injured structure in an imaging review [r1,r10].
In a complete tear the sesamoids retract proximally, the proximal phalanx can sublux or dislocate dorsally, and the articular surface of the metatarsal head can be impacted or sheared [r1].
The athlete has pain, swelling and loss of push-off, and cannot load the great toe.

variants.name: Classic hyperextension with axial load
variants.description: A planted forefoot with the heel raised, most often from contact with the playing surface (35.4%) or with another player (32.7%) in college football [r5].

variants.name: Medially directed force (traumatic hallux valgus pattern)
variants.description: If the force has a medial component, the medial and plantar-medial structures and the tibial sesamoid complex are injured more. A relative contracture of the lateral structures can then lead to traumatic hallux valgus [r1].

variants.name: Associated sesamoid injury
variants.description: The sesamoids may fracture, or the synchondrosis of a bipartite or tripartite sesamoid may be injured, with the same mechanism [r1]. See the hallux sesamoid injury page.

variants.name: Chronic or missed injury
variants.description: Unrestrained dorsiflexion after a missed injury can cause longitudinal tears of the FHL tendon, hallux rigidus from repeated joint impaction, progressive hallux valgus or varus, or a cock-up toe [r1,r11].

variants.name: Non-athletic and low-energy injuries
variants.description: Turf toe also occurs in non-athletes. In one series of 12 non-athletes with chronic injuries, all had a positive Lachman test and 8 had a hallux valgus deformity [r12].

anatomy.text: Most of the stability of the first MTP joint comes from the capsule, the ligaments and the short flexor complex. The plantar plate is the thickened plantar capsule; it runs from a weaker attachment on the metatarsal head to a firm attachment on the base of the proximal phalanx, and it contains the two sesamoids. Fan-shaped medial and lateral collateral ligaments give varus and valgus stability. The flexor hallucis brevis (FHB) tendons envelop the medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) sesamoids and insert on the proximal phalanx in confluence with the plantar plate; the abductor and adductor hallucis conjoin with the medial and lateral FHB heads, and the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) runs in its own sheath between the sesamoids [r1]. The sesamoids elevate the first metatarsal head and increase the leverage of FHB and FHL [r1]. In normal gait the capsuloligamentous complex must withstand 40–60% of body weight, and this rises to two to three times body weight in baseline athletic activity and up to eight times body weight in a running jump [r1].

structures.name: Plantar plate complex
structures.role: Thickened plantar capsule that resists dorsiflexion of the first MTP; weaker at the metatarsal head and firm at the proximal phalanx base [r1]

structures.name: Sesamoids (tibial and fibular)
structures.role: Embedded in the FHB tendons; raise the metatarsal head and increase the lever arm of the short and long flexors [r1]

structures.name: Sesamoid-phalangeal and metatarsal-sesamoid ligaments
structures.role: Parts of the plantar plate complex; the sesamoid-phalangeal ligaments were the most commonly injured structure on imaging [r10]

structures.name: Collateral ligaments
structures.role: Medial and lateral fan-shaped ligaments that give valgus and varus stability [r1]

structures.name: Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis and adductor hallucis
structures.role: Dynamic stabilisers; FHB strength tests the integrity of the plantar plate and short flexor complex [r1]

structures.name: Flexor hallucis longus tendon
structures.role: Flexes the MTP and interphalangeal joints; runs plantar to the metatarsal head between the sesamoids and can be injured in chronic injuries [r1]

structures.name: Plantar fascia (windlass)
structures.role: Tensioned by great toe dorsiflexion at push-off (standard biomechanics; loss of plantar plate competence can reduce push-off strength) [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The plantar plate complex is a capsuloligamentous restraint against dorsiflexion. Forced hyperextension first stretches it (a sprain with micro-tears), then partially tears it, then ruptures it completely [r1,r2]. A complete rupture causes loss of the plantar restraint, hallux flexion weakness and instability. The sesamoids retract proximally, and the proximal phalanx can sublux or dislocate dorsally, with impact or shear injury to the articular surface of the metatarsal head [r1]. Sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more compared with the other foot has a high likelihood of a significant plantar plate injury [r1]. The injury most often lies distal to the sesamoids [r1].

The long-term concern is loss of joint motion and degeneration. Missed or inadequately treated injuries can progress to hallux rigidus from repeated joint impaction, progressive deformity and persistent pain [r1,r6]. In professional American football players, a history of turf toe was associated with lower first MTP dorsiflexion (40.6 ± 15.1 versus 48.4 ± 12.8 degrees) and higher peak hallucal pressure (535 ± 288 versus 414 ± 202 kPa) [r7]. Whether this loss of motion leads to arthritis was not established.

structures.name: Plantar plate and capsule
structures.effect: Sprain, partial tear or complete rupture, most often distal to the sesamoids [r1,r2]

structures.name: Sesamoid complex
structures.effect: Retraction of one or both sesamoids in a complete tear; fracture or separation of a bipartite sesamoid can coexist [r1]

structures.name: Proximal phalanx and metatarsal head
structures.effect: Dorsal subluxation or dislocation of the phalanx, with impaction or shear injury to the articular cartilage, or a small avulsion fleck [r1]

structures.name: Medial and lateral collateral ligaments
structures.effect: Injured with medially or laterally directed forces; can lead to traumatic hallux valgus or varus [r1]

structures.name: FHB, FHL and the adductor and abductor hallucis
structures.effect: Flexor weakness after rupture; FHL tears and a flexion contracture can follow chronic injuries [r1]

muscles.name: Flexor hallucis brevis and longus
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and disrupted plantar restraint reduce active MTP flexion; test FHB strength with the interphalangeal joint stabilised and compare sides [r1].

muscles.name: Abductor and adductor hallucis
muscles.effect: Imbalance after a medial or lateral injury can drive hallux valgus or varus; adductor contracture follows medial injuries [r1].

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus and peroneus longus
muscles.effect: The heel-raised, plantarflexed position at injury loads the forefoot [r1]; peroneus longus plantarflexes the first ray. Both are rebuilt before push-off and jumping (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Intrinsic foot muscles and hip extensors
muscles.effect: Disuse in a boot reduces arch and forefoot control and push-off power; maintain with cross-training (clinical reasoning).

cellular.description: Swelling, ecchymosis and pain; platelets, neutrophils and macrophages clear debris and release signals.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised type III collagen. Gentle plantarflexion-biased motion at 3–5 days limits sesamoid adhesions while protecting healing tissue (expert opinion) [r1].
Collagen aligns along the line of load. Loading is increased in steps; a capsular repair is protected for weeks [r3].
Repeated impaction after instability can damage the metatarsal head cartilage and lead to hallux rigidus [r1].

systems.effect: Less great-toe dorsiflexion (40.6 versus 48.4 degrees) changes push-off and the load on the forefoot (case-control data) [r7].
Pain, guarding and avoidance of push-off change gait; pain is the main limit on early loading (clinical reasoning).
Oedema and hyperaemia around the joint produce swelling and warmth; radiographs usually show only soft-tissue swelling unless there is a fracture [r9].
The shoe-surface interface has a significant influence on lower limb injuries, with higher torque and strain on artificial surfaces in some studies [r8].
Pressure to return to play must not compromise care or long-term outcome [r13].

grading.system: Clanton and Ford grades I–III (modified by McCormick and Anderson)

grades.description: Attenuation of the plantar capsular ligamentous complex, with localised swelling and minimal ecchymosis; a micro-tear. The joint is competent and resists dorsiflexion [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Return to play as tolerated, typically within about a week; traditionally 3–5 days with minimal pain and normal weightbearing [r2,r3]

grades.description: Partial tear of the plantar structures, with moderate swelling and restricted motion [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Typically about 2 weeks to recover in one review and 2–4 weeks of lost play in another, often with taping on return [r2,r3]

grades.description: Complete disruption of the plantar structures, with hallux flexion weakness and instability; a dorsal dislocation, sesamoid retraction and articular injury of the metatarsal head can be present [r1].
grades.prognosis: Recovery estimates differ: at least 10–16 weeks in one review, 4–6 weeks or more depending on treatment in another, and up to 6 months in a third. Surgery is often considered, especially in higher-level athletes [r2,r3,r1]

timeframes.summary: Grade I injuries settle within days, grade II within a few weeks and grade III injuries take at least several weeks to months; published estimates for grade III differ widely, so set expectations by the grade and treatment [r3,r2,r1].

healing.description: Swelling and pain. Protect, offload and tape (typical ligament healing).

Early gentle motion in grades II and III once the soft tissue allows; protected weightbearing in a boot for grade II; casting or immobilisation in plantarflexion for 4–6 weeks in selected injuries [r1].
Progressive motion, strength and footwear; non-operative rehabilitation lasts up to 10 weeks in published protocols [r3].

healing.phase: Late remodelling and return to loading
healing.description: Impact and push-off loading, sport-specific work; operative protocols run to about 20 weeks, and full symptom resolution can take up to 6 months in grade III [r3,r1].

milestones.label: Grade I: return to play
milestones.note: Minimal to no pain with normal weightbearing, traditionally 3–5 days [r3]

milestones.label: NCAA football: mean days lost per injury
Grade III operative series: mean playing time missed

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and grade-dependent. Grade I: when there is minimal to no pain with normal weightbearing, traditionally after 3–5 days. Grade II: typically 2–4 weeks lost, with taping and a stiff-soled shoe on return. Grade III: 4–6 weeks or more depending on treatment in one review, and a mean of 16.5 weeks of playing time missed in an operative series of football players [r3,r14]. Before running or explosive activity, the first MTP joint should have about 50–60 degrees of painless passive dorsiflexion (stated for grade III injuries; applied to other grades by clinical convention) [r1]. In NFL players, those who returned within the season did so at a mean of 36.7 ± 28.9 days [r15].

symptoms: Pain, stiffness and swelling at the first MTP joint after a hyperextension injury of the great toe [r1]
Weakness or inability to push off, or pain with toe-off and rising onto the toes [r1]
Pain with walking and an avoidance of push-off, often with a 'pop' at the time of injury in complete tears (clinical observation)
A feeling of instability or giving way of the toe in complete tears
Persisting pain, stiffness or a drifting hallux weeks after a presumed sprain (chronic or missed injury) [r1]
signs: Swelling, hyperaemia and ecchymosis around the first MTP joint, usually on the plantar and medial side [r9,r1]
Tenderness over the plantar plate and sesamoid complex, localised distal to the sesamoids rather than proximal to them [r1]
Painful, limited great-toe dorsiflexion compared with the other side [r1,r7]
Weak active MTP flexion in complete tears [r1]
Instability on the vertical Lachman test, and hallux malalignment (valgus, varus or cock-up) in severe or chronic injuries [r1,r12]

subjective: Mechanism: a hyperextension injury with the foot planted, the heel raised and an axial load; contact with the surface or another player [r1,r5]
Surface, footwear and sport, position and level; whether the injury is acute or follows repeated hyperextension
Immediate function: ability to continue, push off or bear weight; a 'pop' or a toe that gave way
Previous first MTP or sesamoid injury, hallux rigidus, bunion or gout (differentials and risk factors) [r1]
Time since injury and the course so far: a chronic injury has a worse outlook [r1]
Goals, season timing and attitude to surgery
observation: Swelling and bruising around the first MTP joint; hallux alignment (valgus, varus or cock-up)
Gait: antalgic with an avoided toe-off
Standing and walking tolerance in different footwear
palpation: Plantar plate and sesamoids: tenderness distal to the sesamoids suggests a turf toe injury, whereas tenderness proximal to them suggests an FHB musculotendinous junction strain [r1]
Medial and lateral collateral ligaments and the dorsal capsule [r1]
The sesamoids themselves (fracture or bipartite separation) and the first metatarsal head
Plantar fascia and the first ray for associated injury
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive first MTP dorsiflexion compared with the other side (mean 40.6 degrees in toes with a turf toe history versus 48.4 in uninjured toes in NFL players) [r7]
First MTP plantarflexion and interphalangeal motion
Ankle dorsiflexion (calf tightness may raise forefoot load; clinical reasoning)
strength: Isolated FHB: stabilise the interphalangeal joint in neutral and resist MTP flexion at the proximal phalanx; reduced strength compared with the other side suggests FHB or plantar plate disruption [r1]
Single-leg heel raise: tolerance and height
Intrinsic foot muscles and hip extensors
neuro: Sensation over the plantar digital nerves of the hallux
Pulses and capillary refill of the toe after a severe or dislocating injury
functional: Gait and weightbearing tolerance in a stiff-soled shoe
Single-leg hop and sprint push-off, only when pain-free and stable

specialTests.name: Vertical Lachman test of the first MTP joint
specialTests.purpose: Detect anteroposterior instability from plantar plate rupture
specialTests.procedure: Stabilise the first metatarsal above and below with one hand, then apply anterior and posterior force to the proximal phalanx and feel for dorsal or plantar translation. Compare with the other side [r1].
specialTests.positive: Excess dorsal or plantar translation, or pain. No sensitivity or specificity data were identified; all 12 patients with chronic injuries in one series had a positive test, and it was negative in all at follow-up after repair [r12].

specialTests.name: Varus and valgus stress of the first MTP joint
specialTests.procedure: Apply gentle varus and valgus stress to the proximal phalanx with the metatarsal fixed [r1].
specialTests.positive: Pain or increased laxity compared with the other side. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Isolated flexor hallucis brevis strength test
specialTests.purpose: Assess FHB and plantar plate integrity
specialTests.procedure: Hold the interphalangeal joint in neutral and ask the patient to flex the MTP joint against resistance at the proximal phalanx [r1].
specialTests.positive: Reduced strength or pain compared with the other side. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Passive dorsiflexion range and end-feel
specialTests.purpose: Show loss of motion and pain at the end of range
specialTests.procedure: Measure passive first MTP dorsiflexion with a goniometer, compared with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Painful or reduced motion. In NFL players, dorsiflexion averaged 40.6 degrees with a turf toe history versus 48.4 degrees without [r7]. No diagnostic accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Palpation relative to the sesamoids
specialTests.purpose: Distinguish plantar plate injury from an FHB strain
specialTests.procedure: Palpate proximal and distal to the sesamoids.
specialTests.positive: Pain distal to the sesamoids favours a plantar plate injury; pain proximal to them favours an FHB strain [r1]. No accuracy data were identified.

clinicalRules.name: Clanton and Ford grading (McCormick and Anderson modification)
clinicalRules.description: Grade I is a sprain with a competent joint; grade II a partial tear with restricted motion; grade III a complete tear with weakness and instability [r1,r2]. Grade guides treatment, return timeframes and the decision about surgery.

clinicalRules.name: Comparison weightbearing radiographs
clinicalRules.description: Compare sesamoid position beneath the first metatarsal head with the other foot. Sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more has a high likelihood of a significant plantar plate injury, and a small fleck from the phalanx or sesamoid suggests capsular avulsion [r1].

clinicalRules.name: Readiness for explosive activity
clinicalRules.description: About 50–60 degrees of painless passive first MTP dorsiflexion before running or explosive activity (stated for grade III injuries) [r1]; stable on provocative testing and strength close to the other side (clinical convention).

outcomeMeasures.name: AOFAS Hallux score
outcomeMeasures.use: Clinician-rated hallux outcome; used after operative repair in football players (mean 91.3 at 27.5 months) [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Visual analogue scale (VAS) pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at rest and with activity, used in operative series [r14,r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire (MOXFQ) and Foot Function Index (FFI)
First MTP dorsiflexion range and hop and push-off performance
outcomeMeasures.use: Motion and function; dorsiflexion was lower in toes with a turf toe history [r7,r14]

imaging.modality: Weightbearing radiographs (anteroposterior, lateral and sesamoid axial), with comparison views
imaging.indication: All suspected turf toe injuries with significant pain or any suspicion of instability or fracture [r1]
imaging.findings: Often normal, or show soft-tissue swelling only unless there is a fracture [r9]. A fleck of bone from the proximal phalanx or distal sesamoid suggests capsular avulsion. Proximal migration of one or both sesamoids, with retraction of 3 mm or more compared with the other side, suggests plantar plate rupture [r1].

imaging.modality: Forced dorsiflexion lateral radiograph or fluoroscopy
imaging.indication: Suspected plantar plate rupture with equivocal views [r1]
imaging.findings: With complete disruption, the sesamoids do not track distally with great toe extension and remain beneath the metatarsal head; compare with the other side [r1].

imaging.indication: To grade the tear, assess the sesamoids and cartilage, and plan surgery; a useful and accurate tool for plantar plate injury [r1]
imaging.findings: Full-thickness tears show focal discontinuity of the plantar plate with retraction and a fluid gap; sprains and partial tears show thinning or thickening and indistinct margins [r1]. The sesamoid-phalangeal ligaments were the most commonly injured structure in one pictorial review [r10].

imaging.indication: Dynamic assessment of the plantar plate and sesamoid motion where MRI is not available (operator-dependent; clinical reasoning) [r4]
imaging.findings: Imaging reviews describe normal and injured plantar plate appearances on ultrasound as well as on MRI; no accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed [r4].

differentials.name: Hallux sesamoid injury (fracture, stress fracture or sesamoiditis)
differentials.distinguishing: Pain localised to a sesamoid with weightbearing, a fracture line or separation on sesamoid views or MRI, and sometimes no hyperextension event; a sesamoid fracture can coexist with turf toe [r1,r17].

differentials.name: Flexor hallucis brevis musculotendinous strain
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness proximal to the sesamoids rather than distal to them, with a stable joint [r1].

differentials.name: Hallux rigidus or first MTP arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Insidious stiffness and dorsal pain with osteophytes on radiographs; may follow chronic turf toe [r1].

differentials.name: Gout or other inflammatory arthritis of the first MTP
differentials.distinguishing: A hot, red, swollen joint without a hyperextension injury; confirm with urate and aspiration if indicated (standard clinical teaching).

differentials.name: Septic arthritis or infection of the first MTP
differentials.distinguishing: A hot swollen joint with fever, wound or systemic illness; urgent medical assessment (standard clinical teaching).

differentials.name: Proximal phalanx or first metatarsal head fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness and a fracture or impaction on radiographs; can coexist with a plantar plate injury [r1].

differentials.name: Metatarsal stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual forefoot pain at a lesser metatarsal neck or shaft rather than at the first MTP joint after a hyperextension event.

differentials.name: Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury
differentials.distinguishing: Midfoot pain and plantar bruising after axial load or twist; the first MTP joint is not the main site.

redFlags: Visible deformity of the great toe, dorsal dislocation of the proximal phalanx that has not been reduced, an open wound or a threatened skin: refer to emergency.

Instability on the vertical Lachman test, sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more, a fracture or fleck on radiographs, or MRI showing a complete plantar plate tear: refer promptly for orthopaedic foot and ankle review, because grade III injuries often need surgical assessment [r1,r3].
A hot, red, swollen great toe with fever or without a hyperextension injury: suspect septic arthritis or gout and arrange urgent medical review (standard clinical teaching).
Persisting pain, stiffness, weak push-off or a drifting hallux after weeks of treatment: suspect a missed or chronic plantar plate injury and refer; chronic injuries have a worse outlook [r1,r12].
Progressive hallux valgus, varus or cock-up deformity, or a rigid, painful joint: refer for surgical review [r1].
After surgery: fever, wound redness or discharge, calf pain or breathlessness, or new numbness in the toe: arrange urgent review.
Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy or poor circulation with a great-toe injury: refer for specialist review because of the risk of poor healing.

management.principles: Diagnose the grade early with a stability examination and comparison imaging, then match treatment to the grade [r1,r2]. Grade I and II injuries are managed without surgery: rest, ice, compression and elevation, then taping, a stiff-soled shoe or a turf toe plate with progressive motion and strengthening [r1,r3]. Grade III injuries, especially with damage to the MTP joint, bony injury or severe instability, are usually referred for surgical assessment, though fewer than 2% of all turf toe injuries need surgery [r3,r5]. Whatever the grade, rehabilitation under a physiotherapist or athletic trainer is critical to complete recovery [r18]. The evidence is limited to case series and expert reviews with no randomised trials, so involve the athlete in the decision and temper expectations to the grade [r2,r1].

medical.name: Rest, ice, compression, elevation and analgesia
medical.description: The early stages of treatment are similar for all grades: RICE and anti-inflammatory medication to reduce pain and swelling [r1].

medical.name: Boot, protected weightbearing and selective casting (grade II)
medical.description: A walking boot and protected weightbearing for symptomatic grade II injuries. Where MRI shows a substantial capsular injury but the joint is stable on provocative testing, casting in plantarflexion for 4–6 weeks may be prudent [r1].

medical.name: Surgical repair of the plantar plate (grade III with instability, bony injury or failed conservative care)
medical.description: Fewer than 2% of injuries need surgery, typically grade III injuries with damage to the MTP joint, bony injury or severe instability [r3]. In 15 competitive football players, repair gave a mean AOFAS Hallux score of 91.3 and VAS pain of 0.7 at rest at 27.5 months, with 16.5 weeks of mean playing time missed [r14]. In a UK series of 20 patients with turf toe or MTP instability, in which grade 3 injuries were treated surgically, the mean MOXFQ improved from 73.0 before surgery to 28.1 after it, at a short mean follow-up of 7.5 months [r16]. Evidence is case series without controls.

medical.name: Surgery for chronic or missed turf toe
medical.description: Repair or reconstruction when conservative care fails [r11]. In 12 non-athletes with chronic injuries, mean VAS fell from 4.6 to 1 and mean FFI from 102.5 to 61.75, and all had a negative Lachman test after repair [r12]. Small, retrospective series.

medical.name: Biological injections (platelet-rich plasma or autologous conditioned plasma)
medical.description: One review states that there is some evidence to support them in grade II injuries [r1]. No primary trial was identified or verified here.

medical.name: Corticosteroid or local anaesthetic injection
medical.description: Cortisone or anaesthetic agents are not advised in the review [r1]; they risk masking pain and weakening healing plantar tissue (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Early recognition, grading and education
physio.description: Identify the grade with palpation, motion, strength and stability tests, refer when instability or a fleck is present, and explain the timeframe for the grade [r1,r2]. Missed injuries can lead to chronic problems [r1].

physio.name: Taping in slight plantarflexion and footwear modification
physio.description: After the acute phase, tape the great toe in slight plantarflexion to limit motion and provide compression. Use a stiff-soled shoe with a turf toe plate insert or a custom orthotic with a Morton's extension to limit hallux motion [r1]. Grade II players may need taping on return [r3]. No controlled trial of taping or plates was identified.

physio.name: Early gentle motion and low-impact conditioning
physio.description: From 3–5 days post-injury in grade II, begin gentle range of motion with passive plantarflexion to prevent sesamoid adhesions while protecting the healing plantar tissue. Use cycling, elliptical training and hydrotherapy with toe protection [r1].

physio.name: Progressive motion, strength and push-off loading
physio.description: Restore first MTP dorsiflexion and flexor, calf and intrinsic strength, then progress impact and explosive work. Published non-operative protocols have 3 phases lasting up to 10 weeks and operative protocols 4 phases lasting up to 20 weeks [r3,r18].

physio.name: Criteria-based return to sport
physio.description: Return when pain, stability, painless passive dorsiflexion of about 50–60 degrees, strength and function criteria are met, not by days alone [r1,r3].

physio.name: Forced dorsiflexion stretching or push-off loading in the early healing phase
physio.description: Early forced dorsiflexion loads the healing plantar tissue, and the early protocol emphasises passive plantarflexion and protected loading instead [r1].

physio.name: Treating great-toe pain as a simple sprain without testing stability or comparing imaging
physio.description: Missed or high-grade injuries can lead to reduced push-off strength, persistent pain, deformity and joint degeneration [r1].

education: A great-toe sprain from forced hyperextension injures the plantar plate under the joint. The grade decides how long you will be out: days for grade I, a few weeks for grade II and several weeks to months for grade III.
Rest, ice and protected walking help at first. Tape the toe and use a stiff-soled shoe or turf toe plate when you return, and keep moving the toe gently as your clinician advises.
Return to sport when the toe moves, pushes off and feels stable, not on a set date. Returning too early risks a longer problem.
A toe that stays painful or stiff, drifts sideways or loses push-off needs a review. A missed injury can lead to a stiff, arthritic big toe.
Complete tears with an unstable joint may need surgery, but fewer than 2% of all turf toe injuries do.
Stiffer shoes and a well-maintained, appropriate playing surface may reduce risk, but no prevention trial has proved this.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows the grade and whether surgery was performed. Always follow the surgeon's instructions after repair. Published non-operative protocols use 3 phases lasting up to 10 weeks, and operative protocols use 4 phases lasting up to 20 weeks [r3]. Rehabilitation under a physiotherapist or athletic trainer is critical regardless of grade [r18]. The stages below are typical; progress when criteria are met. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single source.

stages.name: Protect & settle
stages.timeframe: Days 0–7 (grade I); weeks 0–4 or longer (grade II and III, or after repair)
goals: Protect the plantar plate from hyperextension
Maintain ankle, hip and cardiovascular fitness
Start gentle protected motion when allowed
precautions: No forced great-toe dorsiflexion or push-off loading [r1]
Follow the boot, cast or surgeon's instructions exactly
Monitor wound, swelling and toe alignment; report instability

exercises.name: Ankle pumps and range of motion
exercises.cues: Keep the great toe relaxed and protected in the boot or tape

exercises.name: Gentle passive great-toe plantarflexion (grade II and III, once allowed at about 3–5 days)
exercises.cues: Plantarflex only; do not dorsiflex [r1]

exercises.name: Double-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Keep the weight through the heels; the forefoot stays relaxed

exercises.name: Straight-leg raise and side-lying hip abduction
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis and keep the foot protected

exercises.name: Upper-body ergometer or low-impact cardiovascular work with toe protection
exercises.cues: Load through the arch, not the great toe [r1]

progressionCriteria: Swelling controlled and resting pain at or below 3/10
Stable on provocative testing and cleared by the surgeon after repair
Walking in a boot or stiff-soled shoe without a limp

stages.name: Restore motion & basic strength
stages.timeframe: Weeks 1–4 (grade II); weeks 4–10 (grade III or after repair)
goals: Restore first MTP motion towards 50–60 degrees of painless dorsiflexion
Restore normal walking in a stiff-soled shoe
Start flexor, calf and intrinsic strength
precautions: Keep pain at or below 3/10 and settled the next day (clinical convention)
Progress dorsiflexion in small steps; stop if the joint feels unstable
Avoid running, jumping and push-off sprinting

exercises.name: Active and active-assisted first MTP dorsiflexion and plantarflexion
exercises.cues: Smooth, pain-free range; measure against the other side

exercises.name: Towel scrunch and short-foot activation
exercises.cues: Short foot without curling the toes

exercises.name: Seated calf raise
exercises.cues: Press through the ball of the foot within pain limits

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise in a stiff-soled shoe
exercises.cues: Even weight over both feet; stop at the first twinge at the great toe

exercises.name: Single-leg balance in a stiff-soled shoe
exercises.cues: Soft knee and quiet trunk

progressionCriteria: Painless passive first MTP dorsiflexion of about 50–60 degrees, or equal to the other side [r1]
Walks 30 min with no limp and no next-day swelling
Vertical Lachman negative or improved compared with the other side

stages.name: Strengthen & load push-off
stages.timeframe: Weeks 3–8 (grade II); weeks 8–14 (grade III or after repair)
goals: Restore flexor hallucis, calf and foot strength
precautions: Use a stiff-soled shoe, turf toe plate or Morton's extension for loaded work [r1]
Stop if the toe swells, drifts or becomes unstable

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, 3 s up and 3 s down, every second day
exercises.cues: Full range with the weight over the first and second toes

exercises.name: Resisted great-toe flexion with a band or towel
exercises.cues: Press the toe down against resistance with the heel on the floor

exercises.name: Step-up and controlled step-down
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Treadmill or track walking, then jogging
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times per week, adding jogging in steps
exercises.cues: Even push-off through the whole foot

exercises.name: Single-leg balance with perturbation
exercises.cues: Keep the arch active and the great toe flat

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise × 15 with pain at or below 2/10 and equal height to the other side
Jogs 20 min with no pain at the great toe and no next-day swelling
Passive dorsiflexion within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)

stages.name: Return to sport
stages.timeframe: Weeks 5–12+ (grade II); weeks 12–24 (grade III or after repair; criteria override time)
goals: Return to sprinting, acceleration, cutting and jumping
Return to contact and sport-specific drills
Plan footwear, taping and load monitoring
precautions: Add volume and intensity in steps; avoid rushing [r3]
Check footwear and surface, and tape as needed on return [r3]
Do not return to competition while the toe is swollen, unstable or painful

exercises.name: Walk–run program
exercises.dosage: 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, 3 times a week, adding running every 1–2 sessions (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quiet landings and an even push-off

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, forward and lateral
exercises.cues: Soft landing and stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Jump landing and rebound drills
exercises.cues: Land on the ball of the foot, then the heel, with the hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Acceleration and push-off drills
exercises.dosage: 6–8 × 10–20 m, 2 sessions a week, increasing speed
exercises.cues: Drive off the whole foot; keep the toe flat and the heel up late

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, increasing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Plant under control, with the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Graded team training and contact drills
exercises.dosage: Partial then full training over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Share the plan with the coach and monitor pain, swelling and toe alignment

progressionCriteria: Full training for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 1/10 and no swelling or next-day flare
Single-leg hop distance and calf-raise capacity at or above 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Painless passive dorsiflexion of about 50–60 degrees and stable on testing
Athlete, coach and clinician or surgeon agree on the return

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for turf toe; the criteria below reflect published review recommendations and clinical convention [r3,r1]
Grade I: minimal to no pain with normal weightbearing; traditionally after 3–5 days [r3]
About 50–60 degrees of painless passive first MTP dorsiflexion before running or explosive activity (stated for grade III injuries; applied to other grades by clinical convention) [r1]
Stable on provocative testing (vertical Lachman, varus and valgus), with no swelling or malalignment of the hallux
Calf, hop and push-off performance at or above about 90% of the other side, with pain at or below 1/10 (clinical convention)
Full training for at least 2 weeks, with a taping, footwear and surface plan agreed with the athlete, coach and clinician [r1,r3]
tests: Passive and active first MTP dorsiflexion compared with the other side
Vertical Lachman test and varus-valgus stress
Single-leg heel raise repetitions and height
Single-leg hop tests (single, triple, side) with pain rating
Weekly training volume and next-day pain and swelling log

prognosis: Most injuries are low-grade. In NCAA football the mean days lost were 10.1 and fewer than 2% of injuries needed surgery [r5]. Athletes with low-grade injuries typically return to their prior level, whereas about 70% with higher-grade injuries, treated with or without surgery, are expected to maintain their level of performance [r3]. In 24 NFL players, 19 returned within the regular season at a mean of 36.7 ± 28.9 days, 3 needed season-ending surgery, and performance after injury was not significantly different from controls [r15]. A later series of 71 NFL turf toe injuries also found no significant change in performance [r19]. Long-term, a history of turf toe was associated with reduced first MTP dorsiflexion [r7]. In an early review, 50% of 20 athletes had persistent pain and stiffness at more than 5 years, and hallux valgus and early hallux rigidus were described as sequelae [r6]. Missed injuries can progress to hallux rigidus and deformity [r1]. Evidence is mostly small and retrospective.
prevention: No randomised prevention trial was identified. The injury rate was higher on third-generation artificial turf than on grass in the NCAA data, so surface quality is a candidate for risk reduction [r5].

Footwear that provides forefoot stiffness and support may help; flexible, lightweight shoes were proposed as contributors in early reports [r9]. The shoe-surface interface has a significant effect on lower limb injuries, but confounding limits conclusions [r8].
Maintain first MTP dorsiflexion, calf flexibility and foot strength; address a limited or painful great toe early (clinical convention).
After an injury, use taping, a stiff-soled shoe, a turf toe plate or a Morton's extension on return [r1].
Complete rehabilitation before return, because pressure to play must not compromise care [r13].
clinicalPearls: Localise the pain: tenderness distal to the sesamoids suggests a plantar plate injury, while tenderness proximal to them suggests a flexor hallucis brevis strain [r1].

Always compare weightbearing films with the other foot. Sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more suggests a significant plantar plate tear, and normal radiographs do not exclude a soft-tissue injury [r1,r9].
Test stability before sport: a positive vertical Lachman test or loss of push-off strength signals a grade III injury that needs specialist review [r1].
Timeframes for grade III injuries range widely across sources (4–6 weeks or more, at least 10–16 weeks, up to 6 months), so set the athlete's expectations early and tie return to criteria [r3,r2,r1].
NCAA data suggest games are the main risk (nearly 14 times practice), and surface matters, so review footwear and surface with the team [r5].
Lost great-toe dorsiflexion is common after turf toe (40.6 versus 48.4 degrees in NFL players), so measure it and rebuild it before sprinting [r7].

forces.label: Ground force under the great toe
Body weight drives forward over the planted toe

captions.text: A football player runs and pushes off on a firm surface.
At push-off the heel lifts and the great toe is bent upward on the ground.
The forefoot stays planted while the body keeps moving forward.
The great toe is forced into hyperextension, beyond its normal range.
The athlete limps off with pain under the great toe joint and cannot push off.
Zooming into the big toe joint, viewed from the inner (medial) side.
The plantar plate is the thick plantar capsule under the first MTP joint. It contains the sesamoids.
It resists upward bending (dorsiflexion) of the great toe.
In turf toe, an axial load forces the great toe into hyperextension.
The plantar plate stretches (a sprain, grade I).
It tears, usually distal to the sesamoids. A partial tear is grade II; a complete tear is grade III.
The sesamoids retract towards the heel, and the joint can become unstable.
On weightbearing X-rays, sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more suggests a plantar plate rupture.
Most injuries are grade I or II and heal without surgery.
Healthy plantar plate: dense, aligned collagen fibres.
Loaded: the fibres tighten as the toe extends at push-off.
Overload: forced hyperextension stretches the fibres beyond their limit.
Failure: fibres rupture, from a micro-tear to a complete tear.
Haemorrhage: bleeding and swelling fill the joint.
Inflammation: platelets and macrophages clear debris and release repair signals.
Proliferation: fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen; the toe is protected and moved gently.
Remodelling: collagen aligns along the load over months, so loading is built in steps.
